Name: compute_conservation_under_compression
Title: Conservation of Compute: Forced Terseness Pushes Reasoning from Token Space into Activation Depth
Short Hypothesis: When a reasoning model is instructed (or steered) to produce a shorter chain of thought, it does not simply do less computation; it partially compensates by increasing per-token computation density (deeper, more layer-intensive processing) on the surviving tokens. Overthinking's token cost is thus partly convertible into activation-space depth, and the accuracy-length tradeoff is governed by whether this conversion succeeds. The compensation is measurable per-token, saturates at a ceiling, and its failure point predicts where compression breaks accuracy.
Related Work: Token Complexity (Lee et al. 2025) shows an information-theoretic floor of tokens per problem and a universal length-accuracy tradeoff, but treats computation as living purely in token space and studies prompt-based compression only behaviorally, with no internal measurement. MTD / Divergence Steering (2025) and 'Sparse or Dense?' (2026) introduce per-token computation-density estimators (KL between full model and a shallow head; mechanistic density) and find density tracks difficulty and rare tokens, but never manipulate output length and never ask whether density RESPONDS to compression. Latent-reasoning architectures (Coconut, ETD, Think-at-Hard, looped transformers, Heima) show reasoning can be moved into activation/latent depth, but require retraining new architectures; they establish that token-space and depth-space compute are interchangeable in principle, yet do not test whether EXISTING off-the-shelf reasoning models spontaneously perform this trade at inference when compressed. Our contribution is the first inference-time, training-free test of a 'conservation of compute' hypothesis: that forced terseness in standard reasoning LLMs is compensated by rising per-token activation-space computation density, that this compensation has a measurable ceiling, and that hitting the ceiling is the mechanistic cause of the accuracy-compression cliff. This reframes the length-accuracy tradeoff from a token-budget story into a token-vs-depth allocation story and is orthogonal to all prior overthinking/early-exit work.
Abstract: Reasoning language models spend many tokens 'thinking,' and a universal tradeoff links shorter chains of thought to lower accuracy. This tradeoff is usually explained purely in token space: fewer tokens mean less computation. We propose a different, mechanistic account—conservation of compute. We hypothesize that when a model is forced to be terse, it partially compensates by pushing computation from token space into activation space: each surviving token undergoes deeper, more layer-intensive processing. Overthinking's cost is thus partly convertible into per-token depth, and the accuracy-length curve is governed by whether this conversion succeeds and by an activation-space ceiling beyond which it cannot. Across GSM8K, MATH500, AIME, and GPQA on open reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1 distills 1.5B-14B, Qwen3), we measure per-token computation density using logit-lens convergence depth and a shallow-head KL estimator (MTD). We first show that under matched problems, compressing the chain of thought (via prompted terseness and via a length-steering direction) systematically raises per-token density on the retained tokens—quantifying a compute-conservation coefficient (density gain per token removed). We test whether this coefficient predicts which problems compress losslessly versus which fall off the accuracy cliff, better than token count or Token-Complexity baselines. We then causally probe the ceiling: we cap per-token depth (early-exit forcing) during compressed generation and show accuracy collapses precisely when compensation is blocked, and conversely that adding recurrent latent iterations (looping reasoning layers) restores accuracy under compression. Our work reframes the length-accuracy tradeoff as token-vs-depth compute allocation and yields an interpretable predictor of safe compression.
Experiments:
1) Per-token density instrumentation: For a reasoning trace, compute two per-token computation-density measures at each generated token: (a) logit-lens convergence depth = earliest layer after which the argmax equals the final output and stays stable; (b) MTD = KL divergence between the full-model next-token distribution and a shallow-head (or early-layer logit-lens) distribution. Validate both track difficulty (higher on numeric/answer tokens, on rare tokens, on harder problems), reproducing prior density findings.
2) Compression -> density response (core test): For each problem, generate a baseline (natural-length) trace and compressed traces via (i) prompted terseness ('use as few words as possible', 'answer in <=N tokens') at several strengths and (ii) steering along a length/verbosity direction (difference-of-means between short and long traces). Measure, on the RETAINED / semantically-matched tokens, whether mean per-token density rises as length drops. Define the compute-conservation coefficient k = increase in mean per-token density per token removed. Report distributions across datasets and model sizes. Control: match token content by aligning compressed and full traces on the same computation steps (LLM-judge alignment) so density is compared on comparable work, not just fewer easy tokens.
3) Ceiling and cliff prediction: Sweep compression strength to trace the accuracy-length curve per problem, and locate each problem's accuracy cliff. Test whether the conservation coefficient k and a saturation indicator (density plateauing near max layers) predict where the cliff occurs—i.e., problems whose density can still rise compress losslessly, problems already near the density ceiling break. Compare predictive power (AUROC/R^2 for predicting lossless-compressibility) against Token-Complexity, raw token count, and a difficulty probe.
4) Causal test of the ceiling (block compensation): During compressed generation, cap per-token depth by forcing early exit through the LM head at a chosen layer (so tokens cannot use full depth). Hypothesis: accuracy collapses under compression far more when depth is capped than at baseline length, showing the retained accuracy depended on activation-space compensation. Report accuracy vs cap-layer x compression-strength interaction; control with capping only on narration tokens (should hurt less).
5) Causal test (add depth): Conversely, apply training-free recurrent latent iteration on a subset of reasoning-relevant middle layers (loop them k times, as in ETD/looped-transformer at inference) during compressed generation, and test whether extra activation-space depth restores accuracy lost to compression—confirming token-space and depth-space compute are substitutable in off-the-shelf models. Report accuracy recovery vs number of loops, and token/latency tradeoff.
6) Mechanistic localization: Identify where compensation happens—via layer-wise logit-lens, test whether under compression the answer-relevant computation shifts to later layers / becomes more distributed; via activation patching, test whether patching compressed-trace late-layer activations into an uncompressed run transfers the compressed answer.
7) Practical payoff: Use k as a per-problem 'safe compression' gauge to set adaptive length budgets; measure tokens-at-fixed-accuracy vs uniform terseness and Token-Complexity-guided compression on GSM8K/MATH500/AIME/GPQA (metrics: accuracy, mean tokens, wall-clock, and note that added depth costs FLOPs so report FLOP-adjusted savings).
8) Generalization: transfer density measures, coefficient, and predictor across datasets and model scales without retraining.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The compensation may be small or absent—models may just do less compute when compressed (pure token-space story), which would refute the hypothesis but is itself an informative, publishable negative result clarifying the Token-Complexity picture. Matching 'retained tokens' across compressed and full traces is nontrivial; density could appear to rise merely because compression drops easy narration tokens, inflating the average—we mitigate with content-aligned comparison and by measuring density on matched computation steps, and report both raw and matched estimates. Logit-lens convergence depth and MTD are proxies for computation; we cross-validate with two measures and with causal depth-capping. The depth-capping experiment faces the standard early-exit KV-consistency issue (skipped layers' KV missing for future attention); we report both a clean per-token-only cap and a KV-approximated variant and interpret cautiously. Adding recurrent depth increases FLOPs, so 'restoring accuracy under compression' trades tokens for compute—we report FLOP-adjusted, not just token-adjusted, gains. Effects are likely model-family and scale specific, and the conservation coefficient may not transfer across very different tokenizers. Compression via prompting may change reasoning content, not just length, confounding density readings; the steering-based compression provides a content-lighter alternative.
